narrative:
The model predicts you have a 29% chance of failing your final year. While this is not a majority outcome, it is high enough that the school requires you to take remedial courses to strengthen your preparation and reduce the risk of actually failing.

The three factors that most influenced this prediction were your number of past class failures, the amount of free time you have after school, and your mother’s level of education. Past failures had the strongest effect and pushed the prediction toward passing. You have had zero previous failures, which is exactly the same as the average for students who passed. This is a protective factor, but it was not enough to outweigh the other influences.

Your very low amount of free time after school was the second most important driver and worked against you. Most students who passed report a medium or high level of free time; your unusually low level suggests you may be overloaded or struggling to balance demands, which the model associates with higher risk of failure.

Your mother having only primary education was the third strongest influence and also nudged the outcome toward failing. This is relatively uncommon among students who succeed, where nearly 44% have mothers with higher education.

To improve, focus on protecting your study time, building a more sustainable daily routine, and seeking extra academic support early. Even small improvements in how you manage your workload and study consistency can meaningfully lower your risk before the final exams. (248 words)
